breadcrumb.name: Amps to kW Calculator (and kW to Amps)

sections.h2: Amps to kW on single-phase and three-phase
p: Multiply the amps by the volts and the power factor, then divide by 1,000. 32 A on 230 V single-phase is 5.89 kW. On three-phase the same current in each line carries √3 times more power at the higher line voltage: 32 A per line at 400 V is 17.74 kW.

Reverse the same formula: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor) on single-phase, and amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (√3 × volts × power factor) on three-phase. Choose kW to amps in the calculator above for an exact figure: 5 kW at 230 V single-phase and a power factor of 0.8 draws 27.17 A. The chart below also reads either way, and the 3 phase amps calculator takes kVA as well.

sections.h2: 32 amps to kW and 63 amp to kW
p: A 32 A single-phase circuit at 230 V carries 7.36 kW at a power factor of 1. A 63 A three-phase main breaker at 400 V passes up to 34.92 kW at a power factor of 0.8. These are ceilings for the breaker, not loads to run continuously.

kW is the real power that does work and that the meter bills. kVA is the apparent power, volts × amps ÷ 1,000, which cables, transformers, generators and UPS units must carry. Amps is the current itself. For a heater kW and kVA are equal; for motors and mixed loads kW = kVA × power factor, so the same kW needs more amps when the power factor is low.

faq.a: 5.89 kW on 230 V single-phase at a power factor of 0.8, or 7.36 kW for a heating load. On three-phase 400 V, 32 A per line is 17.74 kW at the same power factor.

faq.q: What is the kW to amps formula?
faq.a: Single-phase: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor). Three-phase: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (√3 × line-to-line volts × power factor). DC: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ volts.

faq.q: How many amps is one kW?
faq.a: It depends on the voltage and power factor: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor). On 230 V single-phase that is a few amps per kW, on 400 V three-phase fewer per line, and on a battery many more. Choose kW to amps in the calculator for the exact figure: 5 kW is 27.17 A on 230 V single-phase at a power factor of 0.8.

faq.q: How many kW is 63 amps on three-phase?
faq.a: 34.92 kW at 400 V and a power factor of 0.8. On single-phase 230 V, 63 A is much less; the chart on this page shows both.

faq.q: How do I convert amps to kW on three-phase?
faq.a: Multiply √3 × line-to-line volts × amps per line × power factor, then divide by 1,000. 32 A at 400 V and 0.8 is 17.74 kW.

faq.q: What is the difference between kW, kVA and amps?
faq.a: kW is real power, kVA is apparent power and amps is current. kW = kVA × power factor; kVA = volts × amps ÷ 1,000 on single-phase (× √3 on three-phase).

key_facts: kW = amps × volts × power factor ÷ 1,000 (single-phase). 32 A at 230 V and a power factor of 0.8 is 5.89 kW.
On a three-phase 400 V supply, 32 A per line at a power factor of 0.8 is 17.74 kW, about three times the single-phase figure for the same amps.
Going the other way, 5 kW on a 230 V single-phase supply at a power factor of 0.8 draws 27.17 A.
kW is real power, kVA is apparent power and amps is current: kW = kVA × power factor, and amps follow from kVA and the voltage.
mistakes: Forgetting the power factor. Volts × amps gives kVA; kW is lower for motors, ACs and mixed loads (about 0.8 of the kVA).
Using the single-phase formula on three-phase. Three-phase needs √3 and the line-to-line voltage (400 V), with the current of one line.
Dividing by 1,000 twice or not at all. Watts ÷ 1,000 = kW; check the answer is the size you expect.
Treating a breaker's kW as the load you can run all day. Long-running loads need a margin below the breaker rating.

how.tpl: {{out.k|4}} × {{out.amps|2}} A × {{out.volts|int}} V × {{out.pf|2}} ÷ 1,000 = {{out.kw|2}} kW of real power, so kW to amps is the same sum turned round. The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are line-to-line and the amps are per line. The apparent power is {{out.va|int}} VA, the load the cable, breaker and any generator or UPS must carry. On DC the power factor is one.
how.text: 1 × 32 A × 230 V × 0.8 ÷ 1,000 = 5.89 kW of real power, so kW to amps is the same sum turned round. The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are line-to-line and the amps are per line. The apparent power is 7,360 VA, the load the cable, breaker and any generator or UPS must carry. On DC the power factor is one.

examples.title: 32 amps to kW at 230 V (heating load)
examples.text: 32 A × 230 V × 1 ÷ 1,000 = 7.36 kW. A geyser or heater has a power factor of one, so kW and kVA are the same.

32 A per line, three-phase 400 V
examples.text: √3 × 400 V × 32 A × 0.8 ÷ 1,000 = 17.74 kW, the most a 32 A three-phase supply passes at this power factor.

examples.title: 63 amp to kW on three-phase
examples.text: √3 × 400 V × 63 A × 0.8 ÷ 1,000 = 34.92 kW, the most a 63 A three-phase breaker passes at this power factor.

examples.title: 50 A from a 48 V battery bank
examples.text: 48 V × 50 A ÷ 1,000 = 2.4 kW. DC has no power factor.

content.answer: 32 amps on a 230 V single-phase supply is 5.89 kW at a power factor of 0.8. kW = amps × volts × power factor ÷ 1,000, with √3 added for three-phase, where 32 A per line at 400 V is 17.74 kW. For kW to amps, choose kW to amps above: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor), so 5 kW on single-phase is 27.17 A.

formula.text: Amps to kW: kW = V × I × PF ÷ 1,000 (×√3 for three-phase).  kW to amps: I = kW × 1,000 ÷ (V × PF) (÷√3 for three-phase)
lines: I = current in amps (per line for three-phase)
V = voltage: phase-to-neutral for single-phase, line-to-line for three-phase, battery voltage for DC
PF = power factor (1 for DC and heaters)

content.safety: These conversions are for planning. A licensed electrician should confirm the cable, breaker and meter connection before any load is added to a supply.
